summary: BBN's host status report for October 26 to November 5, 1971, with daily test results for each ARPANET host. It was replaced by RFC 267.

plainLanguage.summary: A table showing which network computers were awake or asleep on each day.

questions: how did early network monitoring work
subtitle: Daily status of ARPANET hosts from October 26 to November 5, 1971

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators needed to track which computers on the network were available and working each day.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 266 reports daily test results from the BBN Terminal IMP, showing whether each host was dead, refused connection, timed out, half-open, or open.
tldr.outcome: This was the first regular host status report. The practice of tracking host availability continued through many RFC revisions.

today: RFC 266 is historic. It was replaced by RFC 267 as monitoring continued. The practice of regular host status reports remained a standard network operations practice through the evolution of the ARPANET and later the Internet.

sections.title: Network Status Report
sections.content:
RFC 266 is a status report from BBN (Bolt Beranek and Newman) dated November 8, 1971, covering the two-week period from October 26 to November 5. It shows which ARPANET hosts were operational each day during that period.

The report tests most network hosts at regular intervals by attempting to reach them from the BBN Terminal IMP (Interface Message Processor), the central testing point for host connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a report card for computers on the network. It shows which ones were working on each day.

sections.title: Host Status Codes
sections.content:
Each host receives one of five status codes for each test:

  • D (Dead): The destination host is dead or inaccessible, either due to network partitioning or local IMP failure.
  • R (Refused): The destination host returned a CLS (close) to the initial RFC.
  • T (Timed out): The destination host did not respond to the initial RFC within the timeout period.
  • H (1/2 Open): The destination host opened a connection but then immediately closed it or did not respond further.
  • O (Open): The destination host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

A special note indicates that UCLA's IBM-360/91 runs NETRJS (Remote Job Service) but not a full Telnet server, so tests assume NETRJS is functioning when the BBN IMP receives its response.
sections.plainLanguage: D means the computer was dead. T means it didn't answer. H means it started to open but then closed. O means it worked. R means it said no.

sections.title: Testing and Results
sections.content:
The report includes a table showing daily test results across the two-week period. Tests were conducted at a consistent time each day (typically around 1:00 PM to 1:30 PM Eastern Time). The results show the variability in host availability during this period, with most hosts experiencing at least some downtime.

This regular monitoring practice became a standard operational procedure for the ARPANET, helping operators understand network health and diagnose problems across the growing number of connected sites.
sections.plainLanguage: Every day at the same time, they checked each computer to see if it was working. The report shows what they found.
